feedback: If a learner says the faster device must have used more energy, compare the tanks: it transferred energy faster but for less time, so the totals come out close — higher power × shorter time.
Reinforce with the arithmetic: a 2000 W kettle finishing in about half the time of a 1000 W kettle uses roughly the same total energy for the same mug (E = P×t).
activities.intendedInsight: More powerful means doing the same job faster. For the same task, a higher power is largely cancelled by a shorter running time, so the total energy used can be roughly equal — speed of transfer and total energy are different things.
learnerActions: Set two devices to do the IDENTICAL task — e.g. both boil the same mug of water — each running until the job is done.
Watch the higher-powered device cross the finish line sooner, while comparing the two energy tanks at the end.

Observe that, in this simplified model (equal efficiency, heat loss to the surroundings ignored), the two energy totals for the same job end up nearly level even though one finished much sooner; real devices can differ somewhat, for example a slower device may lose a little more heat while it runs.
State in words what 'more powerful' means here: it does the same job faster, not that it uses more total energy.
activities.title: Same-job comparison: faster is not the same as more
